title: The Weight of Responsibility
text:
Responsibility is often discussed as a matter of individual choice, yet most of our decisions are shaped by institutions, incentives and the expectations of others. A surgeon who makes an error under pressure, or an engineer who overlooks a flaw in a design, may be blamed personally, even though the system that allowed the mistake deserves equal scrutiny. Philosophers therefore distinguish between moral responsibility, which concerns what a person could reasonably have foreseen, and causal responsibility, which concerns what a person actually did.

The distinction matters because it determines how societies learn from failure. When blame is concentrated on a single individual, organisations may conceal problems to protect their staff, and the underlying weaknesses remain unaddressed. By contrast, a culture that treats errors as shared failures tends to encourage honesty and reform. Ethical responsibility, in this view, is not only about punishing the guilty but about designing systems in which people can admit mistakes without fear.

questions.text: According to the first paragraph, what is the difference between moral responsibility and causal responsibility?
options: Moral responsibility concerns what a person could reasonably have foreseen, while causal responsibility concerns what a person actually did.
Moral responsibility applies only to surgeons, while causal responsibility applies to engineers.
Moral responsibility is decided by institutions, while causal responsibility is decided by individuals.
Moral responsibility concerns future actions, while causal responsibility concerns past feelings.

questions.text: What does the second paragraph say happens when blame is concentrated on a single individual?
options: Organisations may conceal problems to protect their staff.
Staff are always rewarded for reporting errors.
Institutions become more honest about their weaknesses.
Engineers stop making mistakes in their designs.

questions.text: What can be inferred about the author's view of individual blame?
options: The author believes individual blame should be abolished completely.
The author thinks individual blame alone is an incomplete way to improve outcomes.
The author believes surgeons and engineers are never responsible for their errors.
The author considers institutions to be unimportant in ethical decisions.

questions.text: What does the author imply about a culture that treats errors as shared failures?
options: Such a culture is likely to produce fewer honest reports of mistakes.
Such a culture is likely to make people afraid to admit errors.
Such a culture is likely to support reform by encouraging openness.
Such a culture is likely to remove the need for ethical reflection.

paragraph_translations: Sorumluluk çoğu zaman bireysel bir tercih meselesi olarak tartışılır; oysa kararlarımızın çoğu kurumlar, teşvikler ve başkalarının beklentileri tarafından şekillenir. Hata yapan bir cerrah ya da bir tasarımdaki kusuru gözden kaçıran bir mühendis kişisel olarak suçlanabilir; ancak hatanın yaşanmasına izin veren sistem de en az o kadar inceleme hak eder. Bu nedenle filozoflar, bir kişinin makul biçimde önceden görebileceği şeyle ilgilenen ahlaki sorumluluğu, kişinin gerçekte ne yaptığıyla ilgilenen nedensel sorumluluktan ayırır.

Bu ayrım önemlidir, çünkü toplumların başarısızlıktan nasıl ders çıkardığını belirler. Suçlama tek bir bireyde yoğunlaştığında, kuruluşlar personelini korumak için sorunları gizleyebilir ve altta yatan zayıflıklar çözülmeden kalır. Buna karşılık hataları ortak başarısızlıklar olarak gören bir kültür dürüstlüğü ve reformu teşvik etme eğilimindedir. Bu bakış açısına göre etik sorumluluk yalnızca suçluyu cezalandırmak değil, insanların korkmadan hatalarını kabul edebileceği sistemler tasarlamaktır.
